top_themes.name: Unstable QAS test environment
evidence_quotes: QAS test environment was down for 3 days after the client refresh
Test system transports were delayed again because of the QAS lock window
Could not test the output determination change - QAS transports pending for 4 days

top_themes.name: Stories entering the sprint with unclear requirements
evidence_quotes: Requirements for the rebate agreement story were unclear and changed twice
Acceptance criteria for the dunning story were too vague to test against
Business could not explain the expected requirement for credit limit tolerance

top_themes.name: Mid-sprint scope changes from the business
evidence_quotes: Business added an urgent mid-sprint request for a new billing output type
Mid-sprint scope change - management asked for an EDI order change report
Scope changed mid-sprint when a pricing condition story was swapped in

top_themes.name: Cross-team dependency on FI/CO (solved)
evidence_quotes: Waiting on the FI team to configure the billing interface account determination
FI/CO weekly sync resolved the account determination blocker quickly

root_causes.cause: The test environment is controlled outside the team
root_causes.explanation: The outages come from client refreshes, lock windows and unplanned system copies, which are all decisions made in Basis or landscape planning. The team's actions (booking refresh slots, scripting test data) fixed what the team controls, which is why the test-data problem went away while the outages kept coming. The Sprint 43 escalation is the first action aimed at the real owner.

root_causes.cause: No agreement with stakeholders on protecting the sprint
root_causes.explanation: The scope freeze worked for two sprints, then requests came back from management and the business ('management asked for an EDI order change report'). A freeze and a change log only bind the PO. The people making the requests never agreed to the rule, so it slips as soon as pressure rises.

root_causes.cause: Business decision-makers are missing from refinement
root_causes.explanation: Writing acceptance criteria and a Definition of Ready helped for one sprint, but 'Business could not explain the expected requirement' shows the people in the room can't always make the decision. Requirements stay open until someone with authority looks at them, which is often mid-sprint. The early success of the 3 Amigos sessions points the same way: the right people talking before the sprint starts.

recommendations.title: Agree a QAS availability calendar with Basis and track downtime
recommendations.detail: Get the planned refreshes, lock windows and system copies for the next release from Basis and plan sprint testing around them. Record the hours of QAS downtime every sprint so the escalation to the steering committee is backed by numbers, not just retro notes.
recommendations.owner: Scrum Master with the Basis lead

recommendations.title: Agree a single intake route and a small buffer with stakeholders
recommendations.detail: Instead of a freeze only the team knows about, agree with management that every new request goes through the PO, and keep about 10% of sprint capacity for genuine urgent items. Show each swap and what it pushed out in the sprint review, so the cost of a change is visible to the people asking for it.

recommendations.title: Name a business decision-maker for every story before it is Ready
recommendations.detail: Add one line to the Definition of Ready: a named key user who can answer requirement questions within a day. Keep the 3 Amigos sessions, and at each retro check how many stories actually met the DoR, so it doesn't quietly fade again.
